Chapter 3
Financial Resilience and Adaptation under Sanctions.

Through 2024 the accounts show contraction at firms with foreign or joint ownership and no matching gain at domestic competitors in the same industries.

The decline Other firms Private incumbents Recorded ownership The adaptation boundary Inventories and cash Through 2024

Firms with foreign or joint ownership went from growing faster than privately owned firms to growing more slowly.

National totals show the scale of the decline. Recorded sales at firms with foreign or joint ownership in 2021 fell from 45.9 trillion 2021 rubles to 30.0 trillion in 2024, a decline of 34.7%, while the sales of all other firms rose by 5.5%. A firm without a qualifying statement contributes zero to a year's total. Firms that remained registered with no 2024 statement had held 17.0% of the group's 2021 sales, so about half of the recorded decline is sales that left the archive. Over 2015 to 2018 the corresponding changes were a decline of 2.6% and a rise of 2.7%.

With each firm weighted equally and industry, region, assets, and age held constant, the revenue growth of firms with foreign or joint ownership exceeded that of privately owned firms by 13.18 points over 2015 to 2018 (95% confidence interval, 10.31 to 16.04). Over 2021 to 2024 they fell behind by 3.65 points among firms with positive sales at both dates, and by 8.01 points when firms that recorded zero sales at the end date are counted. The shortfall continues in the comparisons ending in 2025*.

Larger losses at firms with foreign or joint ownership were not matched by larger gains at other firms in the same industries.

Nationwide, other firms' recorded sales rose by 10.9 trillion rubles while those of firms with foreign or joint ownership fell by 15.9 trillion, so gains elsewhere in the economy offset part of the decline. The replacement regression asks whether those gains occurred in the industries where the losses were. Across 572 four-digit industries in 2021 to 2024, the estimated change in other firms' sales was −0.23 rubles per additional ruble lost by firms with foreign or joint ownership (95% confidence interval, −0.64 to +0.18) when a missing 2024 statement counts as a full loss. The interval excludes one, so full replacement is rejected at the 5% level, and it does not exclude zero.

Private incumbents gained no more where the foreign share of their industry had been larger.

Among 1,071,648 privately owned firms with measured revenue in both 2021 and 2024, a ten-percentage-point higher industry foreign share in 2021 predicted 0.11 points higher symmetric revenue growth (95% confidence interval, −0.81 to +1.03). Among the 1,014,695 firms with measured margins at both dates, it predicted a 0.024-percentage-point larger margin change (−0.122 to +0.170). Neither estimate is statistically significant at the 5% level, and the estimates for firms followed from 2019 and 2020 are similar.

Rents from reduced foreign competition would appear as larger gains in these industries. Each firm has equal weight. Gains confined to a few large firms can account for substantial sales while making little difference to the average association across firms.

A quarter of the 2021 sales of firms with foreign or joint ownership belonged to firms recorded as privately owned by 2024, and those firms kept their sales.

Of 45,966 firms with foreign or joint ownership and positive revenue in 2021, 9,266 (20.2%) reported private ownership on their 2024 statements, and they had held 25.9% of the group's 2021 sales. In the 2015 cohort the firms that reported private ownership three years later had held 8.7% of opening sales.

Sales continued where recorded ownership changed. Among firms that report revenue at both dates, combined real sales in 2024 were 97.3% of their 2021 level at the firms that changed to private ownership and 77.2% at the firms still recorded as foreign or joint.

Among the 25 largest firms with a change to private ownership, public reporting identifies 15 as Russian businesses that had been held through foreign companies and seven as foreign businesses whose owners sold or left. The other three cases were unclear. The first group re-registered businesses that were already Russian-owned. In the second, businesses passed to domestic owners.

A firm reorganizes when the profit it expects to recover while a restriction lasts covers the sunk cost of reorganizing.

Adaptation is more likely when the loss is large, when the firm can replace much of what it lost, and when it expects the restriction to last. In the case drawn here, adaptation recovers the fraction s of the loss in each period the restriction binds, and the sunk cost has a fixed part and a part proportional to the loss. A firm adapts when its substitution capacity is at or above the boundary. A restriction expected to last lowers the boundary, a higher sunk cost raises it, and at low enough exposure no firm adapts.

The parameter values are illustrations, as in the dissertation's figure. The accounts record two resources that bear on the decision: cash is a means of paying the sunk cost, and inventories sustain sales while a firm seeks another supplier.

In the dissertation: Section 3.3, Figure 3.1

A higher inventory share predicted higher first-year revenue, while a higher cash share was associated with lower subsequent revenue.

Inventories may have cushioned the first year. A ten-percentage-point higher inventory share in 2021 predicted 0.95% higher revenue in 2022, little difference in 2023, and 0.76% lower revenue in 2024, each relative to 2021. The first-year difference exceeded the average of the next two by 1.38% (95% confidence interval, 0.85% to 1.91%). Of the firms that maintained sales and margins in 2022, 50.4% did so with lower real inventories.

A higher cash share was associated with lower revenue in the second and third years, when the liquidity prediction expected a gain. In the cash sample, a ten-percentage-point higher cash share in 2021 predicted 2.08% lower revenue on average in 2023 and 2024 (95% confidence interval, 0.82% to 3.32% lower). This PPML association is concentrated among firms with foreign or joint ownership. Excluding them gives −0.20% (−0.90% to +0.50%), an interval that includes zero. The comparison of symmetric growth, which gives each firm equal weight, also shows no predicted gain.

The accounts point to adjustment through inventories and changes of recorded ownership, both of which preserve existing businesses.

In the industries where firms with foreign or joint ownership declined, there is little evidence of the expansion by domestic firms that import substitution predicts.

Comparisons among firms that still report probably understate the decline. Among firms in the cash sample, real sales fell by a median of 31.0% from 2021 to 2024 when 2024 sales appeared only in a later statement, compared with 10.1% when the 2024 statement reported sales. Whether the lost sales persist after the restrictions end lies beyond the 2024 accounts.
